data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms as a non-inductive 'critical preference' grounded in the logic of verisimilitude and the aim of truth-likeness, not probability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If verisimilitude cannot be formally defined without collapsing into probability (as Miller/Tich\u00fd argued).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the choice of which theory to test next inherently assumes the future will resemble the past.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper distinguishes between 'probability' (inductive support) and 'corroboration' (report of past test performance). The preference is justified because the better-corroborated theory has withstood more severe attempts at falsification, making it the best candidate for having higher verisimilitude (closeness to truth), even if its probability remains zero or undefined.
